summary: Sets out terminology and requirements for the Drone Remote Identification Protocol working group. The goal is to support remote identification and tracking of unmanned aircraft for safety and security, using existing Internet resources. It also covers making identification information verifiable as trustworthy, both online and offline. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Every drone would carry a name tag that others can check, so people know who is flying it.

subtitle: The vocabulary and numbered requirements for letting anyone identify a drone in flight and check that its identity is genuine.

tldr.problem: Regulators are mandating remote identification of drones, but the broadcast standard sends a bare ID that can be an unsubstantiated claim, and the radio links are too small and one-way for ordinary cryptographic handshakes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terminology and numbered requirements (general, identifier, privacy and registries) for the DRIP Working Group's solutions, such as provable ownership of an ID, an identifier that names its registry, and encryption of private data.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol. It is a requirements document, and the solutions are left to other DRIP documents.

facts.label: Broadcast frequency (F3411-19)
facts.value: Static data every 3 s, location every 1 s

today: RFC 9153 is an Informational requirements document from the IETF, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol itself. The text points to a companion architecture document and other DRIP documents for the solutions.

sections.title: Why Drones Need Remote Identification
sections.content:
Unmanned aircraft (UA) are small and hard to spot: they have small radar cross sections, they are noisy only at short range, they usually fly low (the RFC cites under 400 feet above ground level for UA subject to RID in the US) and they are highly maneuverable. They can carry payloads or be used as weapons. The most basic job of UAS Remote Identification and tracking (UAS RID) is therefore a form of Identification Friend or Foe.

An identifier also lets Internet protocols be used for other purposes. Someone who meets an unknown UA in physical space has no identifier or locator for it unless one is provided, and RID provides one. The RFC sets out three kinds of observer reaction: treat the UAS as taskable, as low concern, or as high concern or unidentified.

DRIP's initial aim is to make RID immediately actionable, especially in emergencies, in tightly constrained environments, while balancing the needs of authorities against operator privacy. The RFC lists the constraints: slow and unreliable low-altitude radio links, battery, size and weight limits, and Observers who may have no Internet access.
sections.eli5: A tiny drone is hard to see and hear, so it should wear a name tag that phones nearby can read, just as cars have license plates.

sections.title: Network RID and Broadcast RID
sections.content:
The widely cited standard, ASTM F3411-19, defines two means of UAS RID. Network RID makes information available through servers on the Internet that Observers can query. It is publish-subscribe-query: the UAS reports to its UAS Service Supplier (USS), which acts as the Network RID Service Provider, and other USS act as Display Providers for Observers.

Broadcast RID sends messages locally and one-way over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, directly in link-layer frames without IP. Internet access is needed only to look up registry information, using the UAS ID as the key, or to use a web-based verifier service. A UA must broadcast on at least one of four data links. The Bluetooth 4.x advertisement frame has a 31-byte payload, which after overheads limits the RID message to 25 bytes and the UAS ID to at most 20 bytes.

That is why trust is hard. Any UA can assert any ID in the Basic ID Message, which has no way of verifying it. The Authentication Message has framing for authentication data but no method, and its framing is too short for conventional signatures or X.509 certificates. One-way broadcast rules out challenge-response protocols. A DRIP authentication payload is limited to 200 bytes.
sections.eli5: One way is asking a website where a drone is. The other is the drone shouting its name tag to phones nearby, with no Internet needed. Shouting is quick but easy to fake.

sections.title: General and Registry Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements apply to DRIP as a set of protocols, and not every protocol must meet every requirement. The general ones include:

  • GEN-1 Provable Ownership: verify that the asserted ID belongs to the actual current sender, even offline.
  • GEN-2 Provable Binding: cryptographically bind all other F3411-19 messages from the same sender to the UAS ID in the Basic ID Message.
  • GEN-3 Provable Registration: verify securely that the ID is in a registry, and which one, even offline.
  • GEN-5 Gateway: let gateways stamp Broadcast RID messages with time and place received and relay them to a network service.
  • GEN-6 Contact: set up strongly mutually authenticated, encrypted communication with the sender, the pilot, the USS and registries.

The remaining items cover readability, QoS policy, mobility, multihoming, multicast and monitoring.

The registry requirements say that public information MUST be available to anyone without restriction by identity or role (REG-1), while private information is protected by authentication, authorization and accounting (REG-2). Registries must also be provisioned with static and dynamic data (REG-3), and AAA must be specifiable by policy (REG-4).
sections.eli5: Anybody should be able to check the name tag is real and see the public details. Only the right people should be able to see the private ones.

sections.title: Requirements for the DRIP Identifier
sections.content:
The identifier requirements describe what a DRIP Entity Identifier must be:

  • ID-1 Length: MUST NOT be longer than 19 bytes, to fit in the Specific Session ID subfield.
  • ID-2 and ID-3: MUST identify a registry, and MUST allow lookup of other data about the entity in that registry.
  • ID-4 Uniqueness: unique in its global space from registration until deregistration.
  • ID-5 Non-spoofability: MUST NOT be spoofable within a minimal broadcast message set.
  • ID-6 Unlinkability: MUST NOT help an adversary correlate over multiple operations.

The registry part and the entity part are one identifier, not two. As an example of how to be self-authenticating, the RFC mentions embedding a hash of the Registry ID and the entity's public key in the identifier. The ID Type field has values 0 to 3 in the current standard, and Type 4, the Specific Session ID, is proposed, with subtype 1 reserved for the DRIP entity ID.
sections.eli5: The name tag must be short, must say which office issued it, must be one of a kind, and must be hard to copy or to follow from one flight to the next.

sections.title: Privacy Requirements and Transparency
sections.content:
The privacy requirements say DRIP MUST enable confidential handling of private information (PRIV-1) and selective strong encryption of private data in motion (PRIV-2). If it travels over IP, that encryption MUST be end-to-end. Safety-critical data sent over Broadcast RID MUST NOT be encrypted where authorized local Observers are unlikely to be able to decrypt it, and DRIP MUST support configurable disabling of encryption where regulations require it. Encryption of stored data and designation of public versus private data are SHOULD items, and a pseudonymous rendezvous between nearby operators is a MAY.

By default, anything that must be sent by Broadcast RID is public, and other registry information is private. The RFC says privacy and transparency often conflict and need balance, and recommends regard for RFC 6973 and RFC 8280. Both public identifiers and protected operator data (PII) are in scope.
sections.eli5: Some facts, like the name tag, must be public so anyone can read them. Other facts, like where the pilot lives, are locked up for people who truly need them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it defines no protocols, so its security considerations are speculative. It lists possible weaknesses of solutions: Sybil attacks, confusion from many spoofed unsigned messages, overload from checking many spoofed signed messages, malicious or malfunctioning registries, on-path attacks on registration messages, and UA impersonation, for example by extracting a private key or carrying a small harmless-looking UA on a larger malicious one.

From the requirements it infers that DRIP must provide message integrity, non-repudiation, defense against replay and defense against spoofing. One approach is to bind the identifier to a public key. This is hardest for Observers with no Internet access, for example in a remote area, since they cannot fetch registry keys, so the Gateway and Contact requirements say when they apply.
sections.eli5: People could try to fake name tags or flood the readers with fakes. The rules say the tags must be checkable, even when a phone has no Internet.
